notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • The Northern Plains lie immediately south of the Himalayas.
  • They extend broadly from Punjab in the west to Assam in the east.
  • They were formed mainly by the depositional work of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems.
  • They are composed largely of alluvium.
  • They are among the most fertile and densely populated regions of India.
  • Their flat terrain favours agriculture, transport, settlements and urbanisation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Plains → Alluvial Depositional Plain

2. Origin of the Northern Plains
  • The rising Himalayas created a large foreland basin to their south.
  • Rivers descending from the Himalayas carried enormous amounts of sediments.
  • These sediments gradually filled the basin over millions of years.
  • Repeated deposition created the extensive Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra Plain.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Foreland Basin + River Deposition → Northern Plains

3. Major River Systems Responsible

The Northern Plains were built mainly by:

  • Indus River system.
  • Ganga River system.
  • Brahmaputra River system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Northern Plains → Indus + Ganga + Brahmaputra

4. Extent of the Northern Plains
  • The plains extend for roughly 2,400 km from west to east.
  • Their width varies from region to region.
  • They are generally wider in the western and central sections than in parts of the east.
  • Their total area is very large and supports a major share of India's population.
5. General Relief
  • The plains appear almost level.
  • However, they have a gentle regional slope.
  • Rivers flow according to these subtle gradients.
  • Small differences in elevation influence drainage, flooding and settlement.
6. Alluvium
  • Alluvium is unconsolidated material deposited by rivers.
  • It includes:
  • Sand.
  • Silt.
  • Clay.
  • Gravel.
  • Northern Plains contain very deep alluvial deposits.
  • These deposits are periodically renewed in active floodplains.
7. Fertility of the Plains
  • Alluvial soils are generally fertile.
  • Fine sediments contain several useful mineral nutrients.
  • Regular river deposition renews soil in many floodplain regions.
  • Extensive irrigation further supports agriculture.
8. Main Physiographic Divisions

The Northern Plains are broadly divided into:

  • Punjab Plain.
  • Ganga Plain.
  • Brahmaputra Plain.
📌 Must-Memorise

Northern Plains → Punjab + Ganga + Brahmaputra

9. Punjab Plain
  • Punjab Plain lies in the northwestern part of the Northern Plains.
  • It was formed mainly by the Indus and its tributaries.
  • A major portion of the historic Punjab Plain now lies in Pakistan.
  • The Indian portion lies mainly in Punjab, Haryana and adjoining regions.
10. Indus Tributaries and Punjab Plain

Important rivers include:

  • Jhelum.
  • Chenab.
  • Ravi.
  • Beas.
  • Sutlej.

These rivers contributed to the formation of the Punjab Plain.

11. Meaning of Punjab
  • Punjab is derived from Persian words:
  • Panj → Five.
  • Ab → Water.
  • It refers historically to the land of five rivers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Punjab → Land of Five Rivers

12. Doab
  • A doab is land lying between two rivers.
  • The term comes from Persian:
  • Do → Two.
  • Ab → Water.
  • Doabs are important features of the Punjab and Ganga plains.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Doab → Land Between Two Rivers

13. Famous Punjab Doabs

Traditional Punjab doabs include:

  • Bist/Jalandhar Doab.
  • Bari Doab.
  • Rachna Doab.
  • Chaj Doab.
  • Sind Sagar Doab.
  • Some of these lie largely in present-day Pakistan.
14. Ganga-Yamuna Doab
  • The land between the Ganga and Yamuna rivers is called the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
  • It is one of India's most important agricultural regions.
  • It lies mainly in Uttar Pradesh.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ganga + Yamuna → Ganga-Yamuna Doab

15. Ganga Plain
  • Ganga Plain forms the largest part of the Northern Plains.
  • It extends across much of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal.
  • It also influences adjoining states.
  • The Ganga and its tributaries have deposited thick alluvium over the region.
16. Upper Ganga Plain
  • Upper Ganga Plain lies mainly in western and central Uttar Pradesh.
  • The Yamuna, Ganga and their tributaries drain the region.
  • It is intensively cultivated.
17. Middle Ganga Plain
  • Middle Ganga Plain lies mainly in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
  • Major rivers include the Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi and Son.
  • Flooding is common in parts of this region.
18. Lower Ganga Plain
  • Lower Ganga Plain lies mainly in West Bengal.
  • The terrain becomes lower and more deltaic toward the Bay of Bengal.
  • The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta dominates the southern part.
19. Brahmaputra Plain
  • Brahmaputra Plain lies mainly in Assam.
  • It is a long, narrow alluvial valley.
  • It is enclosed by hills and mountains on both sides.
  • The Brahmaputra and its tributaries deposit large quantities of sediments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Brahmaputra Plain → Assam Valley

20. Brahmaputra Floodplain
  • The Brahmaputra carries a very high sediment load.
  • Its channel frequently shifts.
  • Sandbars and river islands are common.
  • Seasonal flooding is a major feature.
21. River Islands
  • River islands form due to deposition within river channels.
  • The Brahmaputra has several large river islands.
  • Majuli in Assam is a famous example.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Majuli → Brahmaputra → Assam

22. Bhabar Belt
  • Bhabar lies along the foothills of the Shiwaliks.
  • It is usually a narrow belt.
  • Rivers descending from the mountains deposit pebbles, gravel and coarse material.
  • The deposits are highly porous.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhabar → Coarse Pebbles + Porous

23. Disappearance of Streams in Bhabar
  • Rivers and streams often disappear beneath the surface in the Bhabar belt.
  • Water infiltrates through the coarse porous deposits.
  • This is one of the defining characteristics of Bhabar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhabar → Streams Disappear

24. Terai Belt
  • Terai lies immediately south of the Bhabar.
  • The underground streams of the Bhabar re-emerge here.
  • The region is marshy and waterlogged.
  • It originally supported dense forests and wildlife.
📌 Must-Memorise

Terai → Streams Re-emerge + Marshy

25. Bhabar vs Terai

Bhabar:

  • North.
  • Coarse material.
  • Porous.
  • Streams disappear.

Terai:

  • South.
  • Fine sediments.
  • Marshy.
  • Streams re-emerge.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bhabar is north of Terai.

26. Bhangar
  • Bhangar is older alluvium.
  • It generally lies on slightly elevated terraces above active floodplains.
  • It is not renewed annually by floods.
  • It often contains calcareous concretions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bhangar → Older Alluvium

27. Kankar
  • Kankar refers to calcareous nodules found in older alluvial deposits.
  • It is particularly associated with Bhangar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhangar → Kankar

28. Khadar
  • Khadar is newer alluvium.
  • It occurs in active floodplain areas.
  • It is deposited or renewed during floods.
  • It is generally more fertile than older alluvium.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khadar → Newer Alluvium

29. Bhangar vs Khadar

Bhangar:

  • Old alluvium.
  • Higher terrace.
  • Kankar common.
  • Less frequently flooded.

Khadar:

  • New alluvium.
  • Low floodplain.
  • Renewed by floods.
  • Highly fertile.
30. Floodplains
  • Floodplains are low-lying areas beside rivers.
  • They are periodically inundated.
  • Fine sediments are deposited during floods.
  • Floodplains are fertile but hazard-prone.
31. Natural Levees
  • Natural levees are raised embankments formed naturally along river banks.
  • During floods, coarse sediments are deposited close to the channel.
  • Repeated deposition gradually builds elevated banks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Natural Levee → River-Bank Deposition

32. Back Swamps
  • Back swamps are low-lying poorly drained areas behind natural levees.
  • They may remain waterlogged for long periods.
33. Meanders
  • Meanders are winding bends in river channels.
  • They are common in low-gradient plains.
  • Erosion occurs mainly on outer bends.
  • Deposition occurs mainly on inner bends.
34. Oxbow Lakes
  • Oxbow lakes form when a river cuts through a meander neck.
  • The abandoned loop becomes separated from the main channel.
  • They are common features of mature floodplains.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cut-Off Meander → Oxbow Lake

35. Braided Channels
  • A braided river divides into multiple channels separated by sediment bars.
  • Braiding occurs when sediment load is high and channel conditions are unstable.
  • The Brahmaputra commonly exhibits braided-channel characteristics.
36. Alluvial Fans
  • Alluvial fans form where streams emerge from mountains onto flatter land.
  • Flow velocity decreases.
  • Coarse sediments are deposited in a fan-shaped pattern.
  • They are common near mountain fronts.
37. Piedmont Zone
  • A piedmont zone lies at the foot of mountains.
  • Bhabar can be described as an important piedmont depositional belt.
38. Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta
  • The Ganga and Brahmaputra systems form one of the world's largest delta regions.
  • It extends across India and Bangladesh.
  • Numerous distributaries divide the lower river system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ganga-Brahmaputra → Major Delta System

39. Sundarbans
  • The lower delta contains the Sundarbans.
  • The Sundarbans are famous for mangrove forests.
  • The region is crossed by tidal creeks and distributaries.
  • It extends across India and Bangladesh.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sundarbans → Mangrove Delta

40. Sundari Tree
  • The Sundarbans name is traditionally associated with the Sundari tree.
  • Heritiera fomes is one important mangrove species associated with the region.
41. Delta vs Estuary

Delta:

  • Depositional.
  • River divides into distributaries.
  • Large sediment accumulation.

Estuary:

  • Funnel-like or tidal river mouth.
  • Usually no extensive distributary network.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ganga → Delta

Narmada → Estuary

42. Distributary
  • A distributary is a branch that flows away from the main river.
  • Distributaries are common in deltas.
  • They differ from tributaries, which flow into a main river.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tributary → Joins river

Distributary → Leaves river

43. Major Ganga Tributaries from the Himalayas

Important northern tributaries include:

  • Yamuna.
  • Ghaghara.
  • Gandak.
  • Kosi.
  • These rivers contribute sediment and water to the plains.
44. Southern Tributaries of Ganga

Important rivers flowing from the Peninsular uplands include:

  • Chambal.
  • Betwa.
  • Ken.
  • Son.
  • They join the Ganga-Yamuna system from the south.
45. Kosi River
  • Kosi is an important Himalayan tributary of the Ganga.
  • It flows through Nepal and Bihar.
  • It has historically shifted its course across the plains.
  • It is notorious for severe flooding in Bihar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kosi → Bihar Floods

46. "Sorrow of Bihar"
  • Kosi is traditionally called the "Sorrow of Bihar" because of recurrent floods and channel shifts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sorrow of Bihar → Kosi

47. Damodar River
  • Damodar flows through Jharkhand and West Bengal.
  • It was historically associated with destructive floods.
  • It was traditionally called the "Sorrow of Bengal."
📌 Must-Memorise

Sorrow of Bengal → Damodar

48. Brahmaputra Sedimentation
  • Brahmaputra carries heavy sediment loads from young mountains.
  • Deposition forms sandbars and islands.
  • Bank erosion and channel migration are common.
  • Flooding is frequent during the monsoon.
49. Punjab Plain Drainage
  • Much of the Punjab Plain is drained by rivers of the Indus system.
  • Extensive irrigation supports agriculture.
  • Canal irrigation is especially important.
50. Ganga Plain Drainage
  • Ganga and its tributaries form a dense drainage network.
  • River gradients are low across much of the plain.
  • Meanders and floodplains are common.
51. Brahmaputra Valley Relief
  • Assam's Brahmaputra Valley is surrounded by hills.
  • The valley is relatively narrow compared with the Ganga Plain.
  • Numerous tributaries descend from surrounding mountains.
52. Fertile Agricultural Region

Major crops of the Northern Plains include:

  • Rice.
  • Wheat.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Maize.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Jute in eastern regions.
53. Wheat Belt
  • Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh are major wheat-growing areas.
  • Irrigation and fertile alluvial soils support high production.
  • Winter conditions favour rabi wheat.
54. Rice Belt
  • Rice becomes increasingly important toward the wetter eastern plains.
  • Bihar, West Bengal and Assam have extensive rice cultivation.
  • Rice is also important in irrigated parts of north India.
55. Sugarcane
  • Uttar Pradesh is a major sugarcane-producing region.
  • Fertile plains, irrigation and warm growing conditions support cultivation.
56. Jute
  • Jute cultivation is strongly associated with the lower Ganga-Brahmaputra deltaic region.
  • West Bengal is especially important.
  • Warm, humid climate and alluvial soils are favourable.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jute → Lower Ganga Plain → West Bengal

57. Population Density
  • The Northern Plains support some of India's highest population densities.
  • Reasons include:
  • Fertile soils.
  • Water availability.
  • Flat terrain.
  • Agriculture.
  • Transport.
  • Urban development.
58. Urban Centres

Major cities located within or near the Northern Plains include:

  • Delhi.
  • Chandigarh.
  • Lucknow.
  • Kanpur.
  • Prayagraj.
  • Varanasi.
  • Patna.
  • Kolkata.
  • Guwahati.
59. Transport Advantages
  • Flat terrain makes road and railway construction easier.
  • Major transport corridors run across the plains.
  • Navigable rivers also have transport potential in some sectors.
60. Inland Waterways
  • Ganga and Brahmaputra systems are important for inland navigation.
  • Flat gradients and large river channels favour navigation in selected stretches.
61. Irrigation

Important irrigation sources include:

  • Canals.
  • Tube wells.
  • Wells.
  • River projects.
  • Alluvial aquifers provide abundant groundwater in many regions.
62. Groundwater
  • Thick alluvial deposits can store large quantities of groundwater.
  • Shallow aquifers are widely used for irrigation and domestic supply.
  • Excess extraction can lower groundwater levels.
63. Flood Hazard
  • Flooding is one of the major hazards of the Northern Plains.
  • Causes include:
  • Heavy monsoon rainfall.
  • High Himalayan runoff.
  • Sediment deposition.
  • River-channel shifts.
  • Embankment failures.
  • Poor drainage.
64. Flood-Prone Regions

Particularly flood-prone areas include:

  • Bihar plains.
  • Eastern Uttar Pradesh.
  • Assam's Brahmaputra Valley.
  • Parts of West Bengal.
65. Riverbank Erosion
  • Riverbank erosion is especially serious along the Brahmaputra and major Ganga tributaries.
  • Entire settlements and agricultural fields may be lost due to channel migration.
66. Embankments
  • Embankments are constructed to contain river floods.
  • They can protect areas from moderate flooding.
  • However, breaches can cause severe local damage.
  • Sediment accumulation within embanked channels can also create long-term problems.
67. Waterlogging
  • Waterlogging occurs where the water table rises close to the surface.
  • Poor drainage and excessive irrigation can contribute.
  • Waterlogging reduces soil aeration and crop productivity.
68. Salinity Problems
  • In some irrigated areas, evaporation leaves salts near the soil surface.
  • Poor drainage can worsen soil salinity.
  • Such problems occur particularly in arid and semi-arid parts of the northwestern plains.
69. Plains and Green Revolution
  • Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh became major centres of the Green Revolution.
  • Fertile alluvial soils, irrigation, HYV seeds and fertilisers supported intensive agriculture.
  • Agriculture will be covered in detail later.
70. Punjab-Haryana Plain

Key characteristics include:

  • Flat terrain.
  • Extensive irrigation.
  • Wheat-rice agriculture.
  • High agricultural productivity.
  • Dense road and canal networks.
71. Uttar Pradesh Plain
  • Uttar Pradesh occupies a large portion of the Ganga Plain.
  • Major rivers include Ganga, Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gomti and others.
  • Agriculture and population density are high.
72. Bihar Plain
  • Bihar is crossed by several Himalayan rivers.
  • Kosi, Gandak and Ghaghara contribute to flooding.
  • The plains are highly fertile.
  • River-channel instability is a major challenge.
73. West Bengal Plain
  • West Bengal contains the lower Ganga Plain and deltaic region.
  • Jute and rice are important crops.
  • The southern portion merges into the Sundarbans delta.
74. Assam Plain
  • Assam's main lowland is the Brahmaputra Valley.
  • Tea is extensively grown on suitable uplands and slopes adjoining the valley rather than floodplains alone.
  • Rice is important in the plains.
  • Floods are recurrent.
75. Old and New Alluvium Distribution
  • Bhangar generally occupies slightly elevated areas.
  • Khadar occupies lower active floodplains.
  • Both occur extensively in the Ganga Plain.
  • Khadar is periodically renewed by fresh sediment.
76. Khadar Fertility
  • Frequent deposition of fine silt replenishes minerals.
  • Therefore, Khadar is generally highly suitable for agriculture.
  • However, active floodplains also face repeated flood risk.
77. Bhangar Surface
  • Bhangar surfaces are older and usually lie above modern flood levels.
  • They may have mature soils.
  • Kankar accumulation can locally reduce fertility.
78. Terai Agriculture
  • Many former swampy Terai areas have been drained and cleared.
  • They now support agriculture and settlement.
  • The region still has high groundwater and moisture.
79. Terai Forests
  • Historically, the Terai supported dense forests and grasslands.
  • Important wildlife habitats remain in protected areas along the Himalayan foothills.
80. Bhabar Agriculture
  • Bhabar's coarse deposits are highly permeable.
  • Surface water is less available.
  • Agriculture is therefore less intensive than in the Terai immediately south.
81. Northern Plains and Rivers
  • Rivers are not merely boundaries of the plains.
  • They continually reshape them through erosion and deposition.
  • River migration produces new floodplains, levees and abandoned channels.
82. Meander Cut-Off

Typical sequence:

  • River bend enlarges.
  • Neck becomes narrow.
  • River cuts across the neck during high flow.
  • Old bend is abandoned.
  • Oxbow lake forms.
83. Riverine Islands and Chars
  • Temporary or semi-permanent sediment islands form within large rivers.
  • In the Brahmaputra and Ganga systems, such depositional islands are often called chars in regional usage.
  • They are highly vulnerable to floods and erosion.
84. Deltaic Islands
  • Deltaic islands form between distributaries.
  • They occur prominently in the lower Ganga-Brahmaputra region.
  • Tidal influence is strong in the Sundarbans.
85. Tidal Action in Lower Delta
  • Lower delta channels are influenced by tides.
  • Salinity increases toward the coast.
  • Mangrove vegetation is adapted to tidal and brackish conditions.
86. Northern Plains and Natural Vegetation
  • Much original natural vegetation has been removed for agriculture and settlement.
  • Terai forests, riverine vegetation and wetlands remain important ecological habitats.
87. Wetlands
  • Floodplains contain numerous wetlands, marshes, oxbow lakes and seasonal water bodies.
  • They store floodwater.
  • They support fish, birds and other biodiversity.
88. Importance of Wetlands

Floodplain wetlands:

  • Reduce flood peaks.
  • Recharge groundwater.
  • Provide fisheries.
  • Support migratory birds.
  • Store sediments and nutrients.
89. Plain Formation Is Continuing
  • Northern Plains are not geologically static.
  • Rivers continue to deposit sediments.
  • Channels continue to migrate.
  • Floodplains and deltas continue to evolve.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Northern Plains → Active Depositional Landscape

90. Northern Plains and Himalayas
  • The plains depend strongly on sediment supplied by the Himalayas.
  • Young Himalayan rocks erode rapidly.
  • Rivers transport the eroded material southward.
  • Thus, Himalayan uplift and plain formation are closely connected.
91. Indo-Gangetic Plain
  • The term Indo-Gangetic Plain broadly refers to extensive plains associated with the Indus and Ganga systems.
  • In broader geographical usage, the Brahmaputra Plain is often discussed along with this northern alluvial system.
92. Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra Plain
  • This term highlights the continuity of the entire northern alluvial belt.
  • It extends across India and neighbouring South Asian regions.
  • It is one of the world's major riverine lowlands.
93. Importance to Indian Economy

The Northern Plains contribute strongly to:

  • Food-grain production.
  • Sugarcane cultivation.
  • Jute production.
  • Dairy and livestock.
  • Industry.
  • Trade.
  • Urban growth.
  • Transport.
94. Historical Importance
  • River valleys provided fertile land and water.
  • Many ancient settlements and kingdoms developed in the plains.
  • The Ganga Plain became one of India's major historical and cultural cores.
95. Strategic Importance
  • Northwestern plains historically formed an important land approach into the subcontinent.
  • Modern plains support major transport and defence corridors.
  • River systems are important for water security.
96. Northern Plains vs Peninsular Plateau

Northern Plains:

  • Young.
  • Alluvial.
  • Flat.
  • Depositional.
  • Fertile.

Peninsular Plateau:

  • Ancient.
  • Crystalline.
  • Uneven.
  • Erosional/structural.
  • Mineral-rich.
97. Northern Plains vs Himalayan Region

Northern Plains:

  • Low elevation.
  • Dense population.
  • Extensive agriculture.
  • Easier transport.

Himalayas:

  • High relief.
  • Sparse population at high altitude.
  • Steep slopes.
  • Difficult transport.
98. Map-Based Facts to Locate

Locate:

  • Punjab Plain.
  • Ganga Plain.
  • Brahmaputra Plain.
  • Bhabar.
  • Terai.
  • Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
  • Kosi.
  • Damodar.
  • Majuli.
  • Sundarbans.
  • Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta.
99. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Northern Plains → Alluvium.
  • Bhabar → Pebbles.
  • Terai → Marsh.
  • Bhangar → Old alluvium.
  • Khadar → New alluvium.
  • Bhangar → Kankar.
  • Ganga-Yamuna → Doab.
  • Kosi → Sorrow of Bihar.
  • Damodar → Sorrow of Bengal.
  • Majuli → Brahmaputra.
  • Sundarbans → Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta.
  • West Bengal → Jute.
  • Punjab-Haryana → Wheat.
  • Assam Valley → Brahmaputra Plain.
100. TNPSC Traps
  • Northern Plains are depositional, not erosional plains.
  • They were formed mainly by Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems.
  • Alluvium is river-deposited material.
  • Bhabar lies immediately south of Shiwaliks.
  • Terai lies south of Bhabar.
  • Streams disappear in Bhabar.
  • Streams re-emerge in Terai.
  • Bhabar is coarse and porous.
  • Terai is marshy.
  • Bhangar is older alluvium.
  • Khadar is newer alluvium.
  • Kankar is associated mainly with Bhangar.
  • Khadar is renewed by floods.
  • A doab lies between two rivers.
  • Ganga-Yamuna Doab lies mainly in Uttar Pradesh.
  • Punjab means land of five rivers.
  • Kosi is called Sorrow of Bihar.
  • Damodar is traditionally called Sorrow of Bengal.
  • Majuli is associated with Brahmaputra.
  • Oxbow lake forms from a cut-off meander.
  • Brahmaputra often has braided channels.
  • Tributary joins a main river.
  • Distributary leaves a main river.
  • Sundarbans lies in a deltaic environment.
  • Eastern lower plains are wetter than northwestern plains.
  • Northern Plains have high agricultural and population density.
  • Flooding is both a source of fertile sediment and a major hazard.
  • Bhangar and Khadar are not different rivers; they are types of alluvium.
101. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Northern Plain → Alluvial.
  • Rivers → Indus-Ganga-Brahmaputra.
  • Punjab → Five rivers.
  • Doab → Between two rivers.
  • Bhabar → Pebbles.
  • Bhabar → Streams disappear.
  • Terai → Marsh.
  • Terai → Streams reappear.
  • Bhangar → Old.
  • Khadar → New.
  • Bhangar → Kankar.
  • Meander cut-off → Oxbow.
  • Brahmaputra → Braided.
  • Kosi → Bihar sorrow.
  • Damodar → Bengal sorrow.
  • Majuli → Assam.
  • Sundarbans → Delta.
  • Jute → Bengal.
  • Wheat → Punjab-Haryana.
  • Plains → Dense population.

  • Kosi is called? → Sorrow of Bihar.
  • Damodar is traditionally called? → Sorrow of Bengal.
  • Majuli is associated with? → Brahmaputra River.
  • Majuli is in? → Assam.
  • Major crop of Punjab-Haryana plains? → Wheat.
  • Major crop of wetter eastern plains? → Rice.
  • Jute is strongly associated with? → West Bengal and lower Ganga Plain.
  • Why are Northern Plains densely populated? → Fertile soil, water, flat land, agriculture and transport.
  • Why are plains suitable for transport? → Flat relief.
  • Major natural hazard? → Flooding.
  • Regions especially flood-prone? → Bihar, Assam, eastern Uttar Pradesh and parts of West Bengal.
  • What is waterlogging? → Water table rises close to land surface.
  • Why can salinity develop in irrigated plains? → Excess irrigation, poor drainage and evaporation.
  • Green Revolution core regions in Northern Plains? → Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
  • Are Northern Plains geologically old like the Peninsular Plateau? → No.
  • Northern Plains are mainly what type of landscape? → Young depositional landscape.
  • Are they still being formed? → Yes, river deposition continues.
  • What links the Himalayas and Northern Plains? → Himalayan erosion supplies sediments that build the plains.
